questions.question: What is the brute-force closest-pair running time?
options: B) Θ(n²)
C) Θ(n)
D) Θ(log n)
questions.explanation: It evaluates all n(n-1)/2 unordered pairs.

questions.question: Why can squared distance replace distance for closest-pair comparisons?
options: A) It reduces the number of input points
B) Every pair has equal squared distance
C) Squared distances are always integers
D) Square root is strictly increasing on nonnegative values
questions.explanation: Both measures give the same ordering in exact arithmetic.

questions.question: What is the closest distance if two different records have identical coordinates?
options: B) Undefined in every formulation
C) Infinity
questions.explanation: Distinct input elements can occupy the same location.

questions.question: After recursively solving both halves, what must still be checked?
options: A) No further pairs
B) Pairs crossing the split
C) Only pairs already found in the left half
D) Only the farthest two points
questions.explanation: The global closest pair might use one point from each half.

questions.question: Which strip can contain endpoints of a crossing pair closer than delta?
options: A) Within delta of the dividing line on either side
B) Only the highest point in each half
C) All points outside both half-planes
D) Only points exactly on the dividing line
questions.explanation: A point farther away horizontally cannot participate in a crossing improvement.

questions.question: Why does scanning all pairs inside the strip fail to guarantee linear combine time?
options: A) The strip contains no valid pair
B) The strip may contain Θ(n) points
C) The strip always has two points
D) Distances cannot be computed there
questions.explanation: A y-order and packing argument are needed to bound candidate comparisons.

questions.question: What geometric fact supports a constant number of candidates per strip point?
options: A) All strip points share the same y
B) Every polygon is convex
C) Points within each half are separated by at least delta
D) All x coordinates are distinct integers
questions.explanation: Packing separated points into a bounded-size rectangle limits candidate count.

questions.question: How should y order be handled to achieve the O(n log n) algorithm?
options: A) Ignore it and compare all strip pairs
B) Sort only the output pair
C) Preserve it by linear partitioning or merging through recursion
D) Re-sort every subproblem independently at every level
questions.explanation: Linear combine work avoids an extra logarithmic factor.

questions.question: Which recurrence describes the efficient divide-and-conquer algorithm?
options: B) T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n²)
C) T(n)=T(n-1)+O(n²)
questions.explanation: Two balanced subproblems and linear merging yield O(n log n).

questions.question: How does element uniqueness reduce to closest pair?
options: A) Sort by y and ignore x
B) Map ai to its index and test the maximum distance
C) Discard duplicates before running the algorithm
D) Map ai to (ai,0) and test whether minimum distance is zero
questions.explanation: Equal numbers become coincident input points.

questions.question: What qualifies the lecture's optimal Θ(n log n) claim?
options: A) The lower bound depends on the computational model and problem assumptions
B) It says n must be a power of two
C) It assumes input size is constant
D) It applies to every integer machine operation without qualification
questions.explanation: Lower bounds must be interpreted under the assumptions used to establish them.

questions.question: For p=(1,3), b=(0,0), e=(4,0), what is the closest segment point?
questions.explanation: The projection parameter is 1/4, inside the segment.

questions.question: For p=(7,2), b=(0,0), e=(4,0), what is the closest segment point?
questions.explanation: The raw projection parameter exceeds 1, so clamp to the endpoint e.

questions.question: Which formula gives the raw projection parameter t?
options: A) (v cross w)/(v dot v)
B) magnitude(w)+magnitude(v)
C) (w dot v)/magnitude(v)
D) (w dot v)/(v dot v)
questions.explanation: Here v=e-b and w=p-b; the squared segment length is the denominator.

questions.question: If b=e, how should closest-point code handle the segment?
options: A) Return the query point always
B) Discard the whole polygon
C) Return b before dividing by v dot v
D) Divide by zero and keep the result
questions.explanation: The segment is a single point; this adds a guard absent from the slide snippet.

questions.question: A raw projection parameter t=-0.3 selects which closest point?
options: A) The midpoint always
B) The unbounded projection outside the segment
C) b
D) e
questions.explanation: Clamping t to [0,1] makes it zero.

questions.question: How much time is needed to find the closest point among m independent segments by scanning them?
options: A) O(m)
D) O(log m) without preprocessing
questions.explanation: Each segment projection takes constant time.

questions.question: How does nearest-neighbor differ from closest-pair search?
options: A) Closest pair requires a polygon
B) Nearest-neighbor includes a separate query point
C) Nearest-neighbor always finds the farthest pair
D) Nearest-neighbor has no input set
questions.explanation: Closest pair minimizes over two elements of the input set; nearest-neighbor fixes the query.
